newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine T-bills to maintain downward glide-traders.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine T-bills to maintain downward glide-traders.

text.p: Traders said on Monday they expected Ukrainian treasury bill yields to dip slightly at auctions this week, part of a gentle decline spurred by recent increased interest from Western buyers.

"There is increased demand from the West, so I see yields declining at the same rate," said Patricia Bartholomew, senior analyst at WoodCommerz. "Yields will slide just a little but there won't be a big bounce."

Bartholomew said Ukraine's imminent signing of a stand-by deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which government officials have put at $750 million for one year, served to increase foreign investor confidence.

Six-month bills remained at 20.13 percent, nine-month bills fell to 27.52 percent from 27.70 percent, 12-month bills slipped to 29.16 percent from 29.65 percent and 18-month bills eased to 32.42 from 34.45 percent at the most recent auctions.
"They can't push 12-month yields much lower or they'll get to the nine-month rate," Bartholomew added. "There may be a slight drop in the nine-month."
She said the hryvnia, unchanged at 1.8570 to the dollar on the Ukrainian Interbank Currency Exchange on Monday, would probably stay at the level it has maintained since mid-June.
"I don't expect major developments until the fall, when exporters will get paid in dollars," she said.

A Western banker said the gradual drop in Ukrainian T-bill yields was frustrating Western investors seeking alternatives for their money to Russia, where yields fell to 17.9 percent from 18.2 percent late last week.
"Westerners do not know where to go," he said.

Ukrainian officials said at the weekend they hoped to conclude a deal with the IMF this week for the stand-by credit, to be utilised until the former Soviet republic met conditions for a larger, long-term loan at the end of 1997 or early 1998.
Dealer Alexander Okhrymenko for Banque Societe Generale said the Finance Ministry would continue bringing yields down because it did not need large amounts to cover payments from previous sales.
He also said a central bank announcement last week that it may lower the refinancing rate from 18 percent next month would also contribute to downwardly gliding yields.

"The Finance Ministry's chief task is to lower yields, and because there are rumours the refinancing rate will be lowered in August they will be able to continue what they've been doing," Okhrymenko said.
He said President Leonid Kuchma's government reshuffle late last week would have little influence on the T-bill market.
"The biggest problem for foreign investors is lack of clear tax laws on T-bill earnings...not the appointment of a whole bunch of new ministers," Okhrymenko said.
The central bank dropped the refinancing rate to 18 percent from 21 percent early this month.
